name: Gondar
info: Gondar, also spelled Gonder, is a city in the Amhara Region of northern Ethiopia, north of Lake Tana. Emperor Fasilides made it a royal camp in 1636, and it became the first permanent capital of the Ethiopian Empire.

facts.founded: In 1636 Emperor Fasilides selected Gondar as his katama (royal camp); the name Gondar had earlier been that of a regiment stationed to guard trade routes in the reign of Amda Seyon I.
facts.where: In the North Gondar Zone of the Amhara Region of Ethiopia, about 35 km north of Lake Tana on the Lesser Angereb River and southwest of the Simien Mountains.
facts.known: The capital of the Ethiopian Empire under Fasilides and his successors; the castles of Fasil Ghebbi; 44 churches; quarters for Muslims and for the Beta Israel; caravan trade from Sudan and the Red Sea; the sack of 1864; the Italian occupation of 1936
facts.today: Gondar is a city and woreda of the Amhara Region, with the castles of Fasil Ghebbi, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the University of Gondar.

t: Fasilides chose Gondar as his royal camp in 1636, and it became the first permanent capital of the Ethiopian Empire, where he, Yohannes I and Iyasu I built castles and churches.
After Iyasu I died in 1706 the city declined as Tigrayan and Oromo power grew, and Ras Mikael Sehul seized it in 1767 at the start of the Zemene Mesafint.
Tewodros ordered it sacked in 1864 and the Mahdists attacked it in 1888 and 1889, leaving a town of ruins; the Italians occupied it in 1936, and it later became a provincial town.
dyk: Charles Poncet, the French physician of Iyasu I, was the first European to describe Gondar, in a Europe where Ethiopia was generally thought to have no fixed capital.
ev: Emperor Fasilides selects Gondar as his royal camp and begins its castle
Emperor Yohannes I orders Muslims and Jews to form their own sectors in the city
Iyasu I dies and the city begins to decline
Ras Mikael Sehul seizes Gondar, and the Zemene Mesafint follows
Tewodros orders the city sacked and his soldiers plunder its clergy and monasteries
Mahdist forces enter Gondar and burn its churches
Italian troops occupy Gondar without a fight
Forces of the EPRDF occupy Gondar in May

sections.origins:
Gondar lies in the North Gondar Zone of the Amhara Region of Ethiopia, north of Lake Tana on the Lesser Angereb River and southwest of the Simien Mountains. The name Gondar was first mentioned in the reign of Amda Seyon I as the name of a regiment of soldiers, probably stationed in Wegera, which guarded nearby trade routes and controlled a restive population.

In 1636 Emperor Fasilides (r. 1632 to 1667) selected Gondar as his katama, or royal camp. The site was about 35 km due north of Lake Tana in the midst of Kémant country, and he moved there from Danqaz. Caravans from Sudan and the Red Sea converged there, which brought trading benefits, and Lent and the rainy season, when expeditions were prohibited, kept the emperor at the capital. Gondar became the first permanent capital of the Ethiopian Empire, set among the fertile lands of Dambia and Wegera. Fasilides ordered the building of the Fasil Ghebbi, or Fasilides Castle, and established five other churches, among them Mädòane Aläm and Fit Abbo. A pleasure pool with a stone pavilion beside the Qaha river became known as the Bath of Fasilides.
sections.growth:
In 1648 a Yemeni ambassador, Hassan ibn Ahmad al-Haymi, visited the palace and described it as a great house of stone and lime. The head stonemason was an Indian named Abdal Kerim, who had worked on the palace of Emperor Susenyos I at Danqaz. In the castle al-Haymi saw beds from Constantinople, mattresses from India, and courtiers in gowns of silk brocade embroidered with gold.

When Fasilides died in 1667, Gondar was so well established that his successor Yohannes I (1667 to 1682) did not seek a new capital, as earlier monarchs had, and spent half of each year in the city. Yohannes built a large number of edifices, among them a two-storey library and a chancery with a tower. Iyasu I (1682 to 1706) built a new castle and several other churches, and during his reign the city's population was estimated to have exceeded 60,000. Caravans from Sudan and the Red Sea converged on and dispersed from the city, and its long-distance trade lasted until the middle of the 19th century.

Gondar prospered until the reign of Tekle Giyorgis (1779 to 1784), nicknamed Fäsame Mängest, "the End of Government". Bahru Zewde noted that French travellers called it "the Paris of Abyssinia".
sections.rulers:
Fasilides, Yohannes I and Iyasu I ruled from Gondar in turn, and the city was the seat of the empire's emperors through the 18th century. After the death of Iyasu I in 1706 it began to decline, as most emperors preferred a life of luxury to politics. Tigray gained importance, since the tolls on caravans bound for the Red Sea could be levied by whoever controlled it, and the Tigrayan warlord Ras Mikael Sehul rose. Empress Mentewab and the Amhara lords of her family held power, and she was regent for her grandson.

Iyasu II died on 27 June 1755, and Mikael hurried to the capital, where he met the child Iyoas I. Oromo influence in the city grew, and it was guarded by 3,000 Oromo troops. Iyoas appealed to Mikael, who became master of Gondar and seized it in 1767. Mikael killed Iyoas and crowned the 70-year-old Yohannes II, and the empire entered the Zemene Mesafint, an era of declining central authority.

In 1841 Wube of Tigre seized the town from Ras Ali II. In 1854 Kassa Hailu took control, and the city assembly proclaimed him King of Kings; as Tewodros he was little drawn to Gondar. Yohannes IV spent the early part of his reign in Debre Tabor, and the court left the city. Italian troops occupied it on 1 April 1936, and after fighting between British and Italian forces on 13 to 17 November 1941 the Italians withdrew. On 23 February 1991 the EPRDF began an offensive against the government in Gondar and occupied it in May.
sections.life:
In 1669 to 1670 Yohannes I ordered the Muslims and Jews to separate from the Christians and form sectors of their own. By 1676 Muslims had settled in the lower town near the Qaha, in a quarter called Eslam Bet or Eslamge, and the Beta Israel were given four quarters, among them Abarra and Kayla Meda. The royal enclosure was known as Makkabäbiya or Fail Gémb. Addebabay was a public square and market, Abun Bet the home of the abun, Qañn Bet the noble quarter, and Déngay the quarter of Christian merchants. Yohannes also ordered that people lending money should not charge interest.

Gondar was a noted centre of the ecclesiastical learning of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and had 44 churches, for many years more than any other settlement in Ethiopia. The city and its surrounding countryside are the homeland of most Ethiopian Jews. In the early 1900s the city traded in salt from the Afar lowlands, cattle, mules and goats from Begemder, honey and wax from Semien and Wegera, ivory and gold from Bani Shangul, and coffee from Kaffa. Italian merchants and a doctor lived there.

In 1994 the largest groups in the city were the Amhara (88.91%), the Tigrayans (6.74%) and the Qemant (2.37%). Amharic was the first language of 94.57%, and 83.31% were Ethiopian Orthodox Christians and 15.83% Muslims.
sections.crises:
In 1770 Wolda Hawariat claimed that Gondar had an epidemic of smallpox. In the reign of Emperor Gigar (1821 to 1830) soldiers camped in the market, plundered the Déngay district and ignored the emperor and the Ečagē, the chief of customs. The missionary Samuel Gobat, who lived in Gondar in 1830, described frequent disturbances in which residents fled to churches. In 1832 to 1833 the soldiers of Ali II plundered homes and seized supplies, and civilians hid their goods in churches. Merchants could not bring goods in, and scholars lamented the collapse of schools.

In 1864 Tewodros ordered the Muslim inhabitants to convert to Christianity or leave, and many fled the country. By the end of that year, having declared Gondar a "town of priests who do not love me", he ordered it violently sacked. His soldiers robbed the priests, burned their residences and plundered the monasteries.

With the departure of the court, the population, well over 60,000 in the 18th century, was said by some observers to have fallen to 8,000 in the 1870s. According to the historian Heruy Wald Selassie, the Mahdists entered the city in January 1888 and burnt all the churches, killed those who resisted and enslaved women and children. They returned in June 1889 and massacred men and women alike. By the end of the century it was little more than a ghost town in ruins.

Under Italian occupation about 2,000 Europeans lived there within two years. By the 1950s the population had fallen to 13,000, with few churches remaining. A severe drought hit Gondar in the 1970s, worst in 1983 to 1986.
sections.legacy:
The most famous buildings of Gondar stand in the royal enclosure, Fasil Ghebbi, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which has been called the "Camelot of Africa". They include the castle of Fasilides, the palace of Iyasu, Dawit's Hall, a banqueting hall, stables, the castle of Empress Mentewab, a chancellery, a library and three churches. Near the city lie Fasilides' Bath, which is blessed and then opened for bathing in an annual ceremony, the Qusquam complex built by Mentewab, the palace of Ras Mikael Sehul and the church of Debre Berhan Selassie.

The Italian occupation of the late 1930s left its mark on the centre. Colonial planners laid out a piazza beside the castle compound and new buildings in a modernist style, and built roads to Azezo, Gojjam and Eritrea. They also built the city's first mosque with a minaret beside the Saturday market. The main piazza still has shops, a cinema and public buildings in a simplified Italian Moderne style.

Gondar is today a city of the Amhara Region with an estimated population of about 443,000. It was also the capital of the former Begemder Province. The University of Gondar, which includes Ethiopia's main faculty of medicine, is in the city.

summary: Gondar, in northern Ethiopia, was chosen as a royal camp by Fasilides in 1636 and became the first permanent capital of the Ethiopian Empire, with castles and churches. It declined after 1706, was sacked in 1864 and raided by the Mahdists, and was occupied by Italy in 1936.
notes: DISAGREEMENT: the city article says Ras Mikael Sehul killed Iyoas in May 1767; the History article says Mikael seized Gondar in 1767 and killed Iyoas in May 1769. I give 1767 for the seizure (both agree) and leave out the date of the killing.

DISAGREEMENT: the History article's lead dates the capital from 1632 to 1855; both articles give 1636 for the selection of Gondar. I used 1636 and left out 1632 as the capital's start. Fasilides is given as r. 1632 to 1667 in both.
Tewodros 1864: the city article says 'violently sacked'; the History article adds 'and destroyed'. I used 'sacked' only.
The 1841 seizure by Wube of Tigre is from the History article only. The city article instead says Wube Haile Maryam, ruler of Semien, was involved in looting in 1830; I left the 1830 detail out.
The decline after 1706 is the article's own explanation (emperors preferring luxury to politics); it is stated flatly here and the editor may wish to hedge it.

Population: over 60,000 under Iyasu I (city article) and 'well over 60,000 in the 18th century' (both); 8,000 in the 1870s 'said by some observers'; 13,000 in the 1950s; 443,156 in 2021 is given as about 443,000 without the year.

Left out: tourism, sister cities, climate, airport, transport, notable people, the 2023 war in Amhara and the Fano offensive (no year printed for it), the 2025 renovations. Poncet is called the first European to describe the city; the dyk follows the article.
The Sahle Dengel dispute of 1833 and the 'Ali II relatives' unrest of 1831 are left out for space. 'Ečagē' is glossed from the article as chief of customs.
The article says the Gondar region's 1994 shares in Gondar woreda; the figures are for the woreda, which I wrote as 'the city'.
